etymology: The apocalyptic visions of the prophet Daniel, chiefly the four beasts and the Son of man of Daniel 7; from the Hebrew Daniyyel, “God is my judge.”
biblical_def: Daniel’s vision, above all the night vision of Daniel 7, is one of the great apocalyptic disclosures of the Old Testament, unveiling the rise and fall of earthly kingdoms and the everlasting dominion given to one like the Son of man. Daniel sees four great beasts come up from the sea, the succession of world empires; then the thrones are set, and the Ancient of days takes His seat, His garment white as snow, His throne a fiery flame, ten thousand times ten thousand standing before Him as the books are opened. And behold, one like the Son of man comes with the clouds of heaven to the Ancient of days, and there is given Him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all people, nations, and languages should serve Him—an everlasting dominion that shall not pass away, and a kingdom that shall not be destroyed. This vision answers the earlier dream of Nebuchadnezzar’s great image, where the God of heaven sets up a kingdom that shall never be destroyed and breaks all the others to pieces. The dictionary reads Daniel’s visions as the unveiling of God’s sovereign rule over history and the certain triumph of the messianic kingdom: the kingdoms of men rise and crumble, but the Son of man receives a kingdom that has no end, and the saints of the most High possess it with Him.
webster_summary: The apocalyptic visions of Daniel, chiefly Daniel 7; the four beasts of empire, the Ancient of days, and the Son of man given an everlasting dominion.

corruption_summary: Dispensational readers force a gap and a future seven-year program into Daniel’s visions; the dictionary reads them as the unveiling of God’s sovereign rule and the everlasting messianic kingdom inaugurated in Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The matter to weigh is the reading of the visions. Critical scholars, denying predictive prophecy, redate Daniel to the second century to escape the precision of its forecasts; the dictionary holds the sixth-century Daniel and genuine prophecy. On the other side, dispensational interpreters insert a long gap into the seventy weeks and read the visions as a chart of a future seven-year tribulation and an earthly millennial program, severing the Son of man’s kingdom from its inauguration in Christ’s first coming. Both err. The Son of man came with the clouds to the Ancient of days and received the kingdom; that dominion is everlasting and already established, awaiting its consummation.

The principle to recover is the sovereignty of God over history and the certain triumph of the messianic kingdom. The beasts of empire rage and fall, but the God of heaven sets up a kingdom that shall never be destroyed; the Son of man—a title the Lord Jesus took for Himself—receives an everlasting dominion, and the saints of the most High reign with Him. Daniel’s visions steady the persecuted people of God with the assurance that the kingdoms of men are under the hand of the Most High and the kingdom of Christ shall stand for ever.

etymology: From Daniel 6:10, where Daniel prayed with his windows open toward Jerusalem despite the royal decree.
biblical_def: Daniel’s windows are the open casements of Daniel 6:10, through which the aged prophet prayed toward Jerusalem three times a day, and they have become a figure of holy courage and steadfast devotion in the face of a wicked decree. The presidents and princes, envious of Daniel, had persuaded King Darius to sign an unalterable decree that for thirty days no man should ask a petition of any god or man save the king, on pain of the lions’ den. When Daniel knew the writing was signed, he did not hide, nor did he flaunt; he went into his house, and his windows being open in his chamber toward Jerusalem—as was his custom—he kneeled upon his knees three times a day and prayed and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetime. He changed nothing. He prayed toward Jerusalem as Solomon had bidden the exiles pray toward the city and house God had chosen; he kept the hours of evening, morning, and noon that the psalmist kept; and he obeyed God rather than men. The dictionary reads Daniel’s windows as the emblem of faithful prayer that will not be silenced by the powers of the age: not reckless display, but settled, habitual, unhidden devotion that continues as before when the cost is the lions’ den.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though the age that would push faith out of public life is rebuked by a prophet who would not close his windows.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle the open windows press upon every age is the steadfastness of public, habitual devotion when the powers forbid it. Daniel did not invent a new boldness for the crisis nor retreat into a private faith that no one could see; he simply continued as he did aforetime, kneeling toward Jerusalem with his windows open. The secular age that would privatize religion, pushing prayer and confession out of public life on pain of penalty, meets in Daniel a quiet, unanswerable defiance: he obeyed God rather than men, and he did it openly, at the appointed hours, as always.

The principle to recover is settled, costly, unhidden prayer. Daniel’s courage was the fruit of a long habit—evening, morning, and noon, as the psalmist sang—not a sudden heroism. The believer who would stand in the day of decree must pray as Daniel prayed before it, with windows open, hours kept, knees bent, giving thanks. When obedience to God collides with the decrees of men, the faithful keep their windows open and trust God with the lions.

etymology: From Daniel 6, where Daniel is cast into the den of lions for praying to his God, and is delivered.
biblical_def: Daniel in the lions’ den is the deliverance recorded in Daniel 6, when the faithful prophet, condemned under the decree he would not obey, is cast into the den of lions and preserved by the God he served continually. The jealous princes, finding no fault in Daniel except concerning the law of his God, trapped King Darius into an irrevocable decree, and when Daniel was found praying they demanded the penalty. Darius, who loved Daniel and labored till sundown to deliver him, was bound by his own law and cast the prophet into the den, saying, Thy God whom thou servest continually, he will deliver thee. A stone was laid upon the den’s mouth and sealed; the king passed the night fasting and sleepless. At dawn he hastened to the den and cried, and Daniel answered: My God hath sent his angel, and hath shut the lions’ mouths, that they have not hurt me; forasmuch as before him innocency was found in me. Daniel was taken up, and no manner of hurt was found upon him, because he believed in his God; and his accusers were cast in his stead. The dictionary reads the lions’ den as a great monument of faith and of God’s deliverance of His servants—the same faith that, the epistle to the Hebrews records, stopped the mouths of lions.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though the modern mind, denying miracle, reduces the deliverance to legend; Scripture records it as the work of the living God who shuts the lions’ mouths.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The matter to answer is the modern denial of the miraculous, which reduces the shutting of the lions’ mouths to a pious legend or a tale of tamed beasts. But Scripture records it as the act of the living God: My God hath sent his angel, and hath shut the lions’ mouths. The same God who delivered Daniel is the God who raises the dead; to deny His power in the den is to deny it at the empty tomb. The epistle to the Hebrews counts Daniel among the heroes of faith who through faith stopped the mouths of lions—not by chance, but by the hand of God answering faith.

The principle to recover is the God who delivers His servants and the faith that trusts Him though the den be sealed. Daniel was preserved because he believed in his God; yet the same chapter of Hebrews remembers others who through faith were not delivered but tortured, not accepting deliverance, that they might obtain a better resurrection. God shuts the lions’ mouths when He wills, and gives grace to die when He wills; the faith is the same, resting not on the outcome but on the God who is able. Daniel served Him continually before the den and was kept by Him within it.

etymology: The eighth-century prophet, son of Amoz; the Hebrew name Yesha‘yahu, “the LORD is salvation.”
biblical_def: Isaiah the prophet, son of Amoz, ministered in Judah in the eighth century before Christ, through the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, and his book is the loftiest and most far-seeing of the prophetic writings, so full of the gospel that the church has called him the evangelical prophet. His call came in the year that King Uzziah died, when he saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up, the seraphim crying Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts. Undone by the vision and cleansed by the live coal from the altar, he answered the divine summons: Here am I; send me. Isaiah foretold the virgin’s Son who would be called Immanuel, the child born and the Son given whose name is Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, and of whose government and peace there shall be no end. Above all he wrote, seven centuries before Calvary, the great fifty-third chapter of the suffering Servant: wounded for our transgressions, bruised for our iniquities, who bore the sin of many and made intercession for the transgressors. The dictionary honors Isaiah as the prophet who saw the glory of Christ and spoke of Him—as the apostle John testifies—the holy seer through whom the LORD foretold the holy God’s salvation of an unholy people.
webster_summary: The eighth-century evangelical prophet, son of Amoz; called by the vision of the thrice-holy LORD, who foretold Immanuel and the suffering Servant of Isaiah 53.

corruption_summary: Higher critics divide the book among a “Deutero-Isaiah” and “Trito-Isaiah” to escape its predictive prophecy; the dictionary confesses one Isaiah, the evangelical prophet who saw Christ’s glory.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the higher-critical dismemberment of the book. Because Isaiah 40–66 names Cyrus and speaks with intimate knowledge of the return from exile a century and a half before it occurred, critics—refusing genuine predictive prophecy—invented a “Deutero-Isaiah” of the exile and a later “Trito-Isaiah,” splitting the one prophet into anonymous schools. The dictionary rejects this. The New Testament quotes freely from every part of the book and ascribes it all to the one prophet Isaiah; the apostle John says Isaiah saw Christ’s glory and spoke of Him, citing both halves. The God who declares the end from the beginning could name Cyrus before his birth; the predictive precision is the proof of inspiration, not the ground for partition.

The principle to recover is the unity of the book and the predictive power of true prophecy. One Isaiah, the son of Amoz, saw the thrice-holy LORD and was sent; one Isaiah foretold both the virgin’s Son and the suffering Servant; one Isaiah spans the throne-room of chapter 6 and the empty grave behind chapter 53. To divide the prophet is to deny the God who spoke through him; to receive the whole is to hear, in one voice, the evangelical prophet’s testimony to the holy God and His Christ.

etymology: Hebrew Peni’el (also Penuel), “the face of God”; the place east of the Jabbok where Jacob wrestled.
biblical_def: Peniel, also written Penuel, is the place by the ford of the Jabbok where Jacob wrestled all night with a mysterious man, and which Jacob named “the face of God” because, as he said, I have seen God face to face, and my life is preserved. Returning to the land of promise and in dread of his brother Esau, Jacob sent his company over the brook and was left alone; and there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day. When the man saw that he prevailed not against Jacob, he touched the hollow of his thigh, so that Jacob’s thigh was out of joint, and yet Jacob clung to him, saying, I will not let thee go, except thou bless me. The man gave him a new name: Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel—a prince with God—for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed. The prophet Hosea, looking back, says Jacob had power over the angel and prevailed, weeping and making supplication. The dictionary reads Peniel as the place of the believer’s prevailing prayer and humbling blessing: the supplanter is transformed into Israel, made to prevail not by his strength but by clinging in weakness—his thigh disjointed, his name changed, his life preserved before the face of God.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though the wrestling is reduced to a mere inner struggle; Scripture presents a real encounter with God that humbled and transformed Jacob.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The matter to weigh is the nature of the encounter. Modern readings often dissolve Peniel into a psychological allegory—Jacob wrestling only with his own conscience or fears. But Scripture presents a real meeting with God, a theophany: Jacob saw God face to face, his thigh was truly disjointed, his name was truly changed, and the prophet Hosea confirms he had power over the angel and prevailed. The Man at the Jabbok was no mere figure of Jacob’s anxiety but the LORD Himself condescending to wrestle with His chosen and to bless him.

The principle to recover is prevailing prayer joined to humbling weakness. Jacob prevailed not by overpowering God but by clinging—I will not let thee go except thou bless me—and he was made to limp ever after, that he might lean on God and not on his own craft. Peniel is where the supplanter became Israel, where strength was found in surrender, and where the face of God, which no man can see and live, was seen in mercy and the life preserved. The believer who would be blessed must wrestle in supplication and be content to be lamed.

etymology: From Genesis 3:15, the enmity between the seed of the woman and the seed of the serpent; the two spiritual lineages of Scripture.
biblical_def: The two seeds are the two spiritual lineages set in enmity by the first promise of the gospel: I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed. From the curse upon the serpent runs the whole history of redemption as a conflict between the seed of the woman and the seed of the serpent—between the line of faith and the line of the world, the children of God and the children of the devil—until the woman’s Seed should bruise the serpent’s head, though His own heel be bruised. Cain and Abel, Isaac and Ishmael, Jacob and Esau trace the parting of the two ways through the generations; the godly line is preserved and the enmity persists. The apostle Paul shows that the promised Seed is ultimately one—to Abraham and his seed were the promises made; he saith not, And to seeds, as of many, but as of one, And to thy seed, which is Christ. In Christ the head of the serpent is crushed: the Son of God was manifested to destroy the works of the devil. The Lord Himself told the unbelieving that they were of their father the devil. The dictionary reads the two seeds as the spiritual antithesis running through all Scripture and history, resolved at the cross where the woman’s Seed, the Lord Jesus, bruised the serpent’s head and secured His people.

corruption_summary: The biblical two seeds are corrupted by the “serpent-seed” heresy, which makes the seed of the serpent a literal carnal lineage and breeds racial and dualist error; the seeds of Scripture are spiritual, parted by faith and unbelief.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption to name is the “serpent-seed” heresy, which twists the two seeds of Genesis 3:15 into a literal, carnal genealogy—teaching that Eve had relations with the serpent and bore Cain, so that a physical line of the devil’s offspring walks the earth. This fable has fed racial hatred and a dualism foreign to Scripture, and it has appeared among the Two-Seed-in-the-Spirit Predestinarian sects and in fringe teachers. The Bible knows no such carnal devil-seed. The enmity of the two seeds is spiritual: the children of God and the children of the devil are distinguished by faith and unbelief, by the new birth and its absence, not by bloodline.

The principle to recover is the spiritual antithesis resolved in Christ. The seed of the woman and the seed of the serpent are the line of faith and the line of unbelief, running through every nation and family; men become children of God by the new birth and children of the devil by abiding in sin. And the great Seed is one—Christ, in whom the promise is fulfilled and the serpent’s head crushed. He was manifested to destroy the works of the devil, and all who are His by faith share His victory over the ancient enemy.

etymology: The written law of Moses, the sepher hattorah; the scroll of the Torah read to Israel and found in Josiah’s temple.
biblical_def: The book of the law is the written law of Moses, the Torah scroll, by which the LORD bound His covenant people and by the recovery of which He repeatedly revived them. Moses wrote the law in a book and commanded it to be kept beside the ark and read to the assembled nation every seventh year. Joshua was charged that this book of the law should not depart out of his mouth, but that he should meditate therein day and night, to do according to all that was written—the secret of his prosperity and good success. In the reign of Josiah, when the book of the law had been long neglected and was found by Hilkiah the high priest in the house of the LORD, the young king heard its words read and rent his clothes, and led the nation in covenant renewal and the sweeping reform of its idolatry. After the exile, Ezra and the Levites read in the book of the law of God distinctly, gave the sense, and caused the people to understand the reading, and the people wept and then rejoiced. The dictionary reads the book of the law as the written, sufficient, abiding Word of God—not a dead relic but the living standard that, when read, heard, and obeyed, breaks the heart, reforms the nation, and revives the church; for the recovery of the lost book is ever the beginning of reformation.
webster_summary: The written law of Moses, the Torah scroll; found in Josiah’s temple and read by Ezra—the sufficient Word whose recovery brings reformation and revival.

corruption_summary: Higher criticism recasts the book found in Josiah’s temple as a freshly forged Deuteronomy; the dictionary holds the Mosaic law genuinely recovered, not invented, and revival flowing from the Word read and obeyed.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption to name is the critical theory that the book of the law found in Josiah’s temple was not the recovered law of Moses but a recently composed Deuteronomy, a pious forgery produced to authorize the king’s reforms—a centerpiece of the documentary hypothesis. The dictionary rejects this. The text presents the book as found, not made: long neglected and now recovered from the house of the LORD, its words striking the king with such force precisely because they were the ancient, binding law of Moses he and the nation had forsaken. Mosaic authorship stands; the reform flowed from a genuine recovery, not a fabrication.

The principle to recover is the power of the written Word to break and revive. Every great reformation in Scripture turns upon the book of the law read and heard: Josiah rends his clothes, Ezra’s hearers weep and obey, the nation renews the covenant. The Word neglected brings decay; the Word recovered, read distinctly with the sense given, brings repentance and life. So it was at the Reformation, when the recovered Scriptures revived the church; so it ever is. The book of the law is no relic but the living, sufficient Word of God.

etymology: The genealogy of Genesis 10, listing the nations descended from the sons of Noah—Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
biblical_def: The Table of Nations is the genealogy of Genesis 10, which traces the families of the sons of Noah—Shem, Ham, and Japheth—and the nations that sprang from them and were divided over the earth after the flood. It is the Bible’s account of the origin of the peoples: by these were the isles of the Gentiles divided in their lands, every one after his tongue, after their families, in their nations; and by these were the nations divided in the earth after the flood. The chapter stands before the account of Babel, which explains the dividing of the one human speech into many; together they teach that all the nations of the earth descend from one family, one ark, one father in Noah, and beyond him from the one man Adam. Paul declared this very truth at Athens: God hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed and the bounds of their habitation. Moses sang that the Most High, when He divided to the nations their inheritance, set the bounds of the people. The dictionary reads the Table of Nations as the charter of the unity and the divine ordering of mankind: all peoples one in blood, descended from Noah and from Adam, scattered and bounded by the providence of God, and destined to be gathered from every nation into the one redeemed people of Christ.
webster_summary: The genealogy of Genesis 10; the nations descended from Noah’s sons—teaching that all peoples are one blood, ordered and bounded by the providence of God.

corruption_summary: The age would either deny the common descent of all peoples or weaponize ancestry into racial division; the Table of Nations teaches one blood under one God, ordered for the gathering of all nations into Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The matter to weigh is the unity and ordering of mankind. Against every racialism that would set the peoples at enmity by blood, the Table of Nations declares that God hath made of one blood all nations of men; there is no master-race and no devil-race, for all descend from Noah and from Adam. And against the modern denial of any God-given order to the nations, Scripture teaches that the Most High Himself divided the inheritance and set the bounds of the peoples—the rise and place of nations is no accident but the appointment of providence. The Babel scattering that follows is judgment on pride, not the abolition of the nations God had ordered.

The principle to recover is one blood under one God, gathered into one people in Christ. The diversity of nations and tongues is God’s ordering, not a curse to be erased; yet the division of Babel is healed not by a new tower of human unity but at Pentecost and in the gospel, where men of every nation, kindred, tongue, and people are redeemed by one blood—the blood of Christ—into one new man. The Table of Nations begins the story that ends with a multitude out of every nation before the throne.
roots_summary: Genesis 10; the nations from Noah’s sons—one blood under one God, ordered and bounded by providence, gathered into Christ.

etymology: The pattern of withdrawing to a solitary or desert place for prayer, as the Lord Jesus did; from the wilderness of Scripture and the Latin retrahere, to draw back.
biblical_def: The wilderness retreat is the practice, supremely modeled by the Lord Jesus, of withdrawing from the press of the multitude into a solitary or desert place to pray and to be refreshed before the Father. The Gospels record it as the rhythm of His ministry: in the morning, rising a great while before day, He went out into a solitary place and there prayed; He withdrew Himself into the wilderness and prayed; when He had sent the multitudes away He went up into a mountain apart to pray, and was there alone in the evening. He also bade His weary disciples, when there was no leisure so much as to eat for the crowds, Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while. The wilderness retreat is thus not an escape from duty but a withdrawal for the renewal of communion that fits the servant for duty; the busiest life in history, the Lord’s own, was punctuated by deliberate seasons of solitary prayer. The dictionary commends the practice as wisdom for the Christian life—the regular turning aside from noise and crowd to seek God in secret—while guarding against two errors: the making of solitude an end in itself, and the despising of it by an activism that never stops to pray. The pattern is the Lord’s: He sought the lonely place to pray, and returned to serve.
webster_summary: The practice, modeled by the Lord Jesus, of withdrawing to a solitary place to pray and be refreshed—a turning aside for communion that fits the servant for renewed duty.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though “retreat” is reduced to mere self-care and rest detached from prayer; the Lord withdrew to seek the Father, then returned to serve.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The danger to name is twofold drift in the modern use of “retreat.” On the one side, the therapy age recasts withdrawal as mere self-care—a recharging of personal energies detached from prayer and from God—so that the desert place becomes a spa rather than a closet. On the other side, an activism that prizes busyness despises solitude altogether, never turning aside to seek God, and so labors in the flesh and dries up. The Lord’s pattern corrects both: He withdrew not to indulge Himself but to pray to the Father, and He did so precisely amid the most pressing demands.

The principle to recover is communion in solitude as the spring of fruitful service. The Lord Jesus, with crowds thronging and the whole work of redemption upon Him, rose before day and sought the lonely place to pray; from such seasons He returned to teach, to heal, and at last to go to the cross. The believer is to follow Him—turning aside from noise to seek God in secret, resting awhile when the press allows—not to flee his calling but to be renewed for it. Solitude is a means, not an end; the wilderness sends the servant back to the work.
roots_summary: Withdrawing to a solitary place for prayer, as the Lord Jesus did; renewal of communion that fits the servant for duty.

etymology: The Jewish family that led the revolt against Antiochus IV (167–160 B.C.); from Maccabee, “the hammer,” the byname of Judas, son of Mattathias.
biblical_def: The Maccabees were the priestly family—Mattathias and his sons, chief among them Judas called Maccabeus, “the hammer”—who led the Jewish revolt against the Seleucid king Antiochus IV Epiphanes in the second century before Christ, when he sought to stamp out the worship of the LORD, defiled the temple, and forbade the law on pain of death. By their resistance the temple was retaken and cleansed and the daily sacrifice restored, an event commemorated in the Feast of Dedication, which the Lord Jesus Himself observed at Jerusalem in winter. This period falls in the four hundred silent years between Malachi and the coming of Christ; the prophet Daniel had foretold the tyrant who would pollute the sanctuary and take away the daily sacrifice and set up the abomination of desolation, and the epistle to the Hebrews remembers the faithful of that age who were tortured, not accepting deliverance, that they might obtain a better resurrection. Yet the dictionary marks plainly that the books of First and Second Maccabees, which record this history, are part of the Apocrypha and are not Scripture. The Protestant canon is the sixty-six inspired books; the Apocrypha, however useful for history, was never received by the Jews as canonical, is nowhere cited as Scripture by Christ or the apostles, and was given canonical standing only by Rome at the Council of Trent. The dictionary honors the Maccabean courage and the history while holding the closed Protestant canon against the Apocrypha.
webster_summary: The priestly family who revolted against Antiochus IV, cleansed the temple, and restored the sacrifice; their history is in the Apocrypha—honored as record, not received as Scripture.

corruption_summary: Rome canonized the books of Maccabees and the rest of the Apocrypha at Trent; the dictionary honors the Maccabean history while holding the sixty-six-book Protestant canon.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The matter to name is the canon. The books of First and Second Maccabees record a real and stirring history, but they are part of the Apocrypha, not the inspired Scripture. The Jews never received these books into their canon; the Lord Jesus and the apostles, who quote the Old Testament constantly, never cite them as Scripture; and the early church largely distinguished them from the canonical books. It was the Council of Trent in 1546, in reaction to the Reformation, that first dogmatically pronounced the Apocrypha canonical—in part because Second Maccabees was used to defend prayers for the dead and purgatory. The Protestant churches held the line: the canon is sixty-six books.

The principle to recover is the closed and sufficient canon. All Scripture is given by inspiration of God; the church does not add to the inspired books, however edifying a history may be. The Maccabean courage may be honored, and the Feast of Dedication the Lord kept may be remembered, and Daniel’s prophecy of the temple’s defilement read with profit; but doctrine is built on Scripture alone, and the Apocrypha, useful for history, is no part of the rule of faith. The Reformers’ verdict stands against Trent.
